sceneHappening: Antioch sends out Barnabas and Saul, a magician in Cyprus, and Paul's sermon at Pisidian Antioch
summary: In the church at Antioch there are prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who is called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. As they serve the Lord and fast, the Holy Spirit says, "Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them." Then, fasting, praying, and laying their hands on them, they send them off. Sent out by the Holy Spirit, they go down to Seleucia and sail to Cyprus. At Salamis they proclaim the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews, with John as their assistant. Going through the whole island to Paphos, they find a certain magician, a false prophet, a Jew named Bar-Jesus, who is with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, an intelligent man, who summons Barnabas and Saul and wants to hear the word of God. But Elymas the magician opposes them, trying to turn the proconsul away from the faith. Saul, who is also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looks intently at him: "You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and all cunning, will you not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord? Now, behold, the hand of the Lord is on you, and you will be blind, not seeing the sun for a season." Immediately a mist and darkness fall on him, and he goes about seeking someone to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul, when he sees what has been done, believes, being astonished at the teaching of the Lord. Paul and his company set sail from Paphos and come to Perga in Pamphylia, where John departs from them and returns to Jerusalem. They pass on from Perga and come to Antioch of Pisidia, and on the Sabbath day they go into the synagogue and sit down. After the reading of the law and the prophets, the rulers of the synagogue send to them: "Brothers, if you have any word of exhortation for the people, speak." Paul stands up and, motioning with his hand, says, "Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen." He tells how God chose their fathers, made the people great in Egypt, led them out, bore with them in the wilderness forty years, gave them the land, judges, and Samuel, then Saul, then David, a man after his heart. "From this man's offspring, according to promise, God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus." John preached repentance before him and said, "I am not he. But behold, one comes after me the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie." "To you is the word of this salvation sent out. For those who dwell in Jerusalem, and their rulers, because they didn't know him, nor the voices of the prophets which are read every Sabbath, have fulfilled them by condemning him." They asked Pilate to have him killed, and took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. "But God raised him from the dead, and he was seen for many days by those who came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem." "We bring you good news of the promise made to the fathers, that God has fulfilled this to our children, in that he raised up Jesus. As it is also written in the second psalm, 'You are my Son. Today I have become your father.' ... He has said, 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.' ... You will not allow your Holy One to see decay." "Be it known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man is proclaimed to you remission of sins, and by him everyone who believes is freed from all things from which you couldn't be freed by the law of Moses." He warns them with Habakkuk 1:5: "Behold, you scoffers, and wonder, and perish." As they go out, the people ask that these words be spoken to them the next Sabbath, and many Jews and devout proselytes follow Paul and Barnabas. The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathers to hear the word of God, but when the Jews see the crowds, they are filled with jealousy, and contradict and revile. Paul and Barnabas say boldly, "It was necessary that God's word should be spoken to you first. Since indeed you thrust it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. For so has the Lord commanded us, saying, 'I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth.'" The Gentiles are glad and glorify the word of the Lord, and as many as are appointed to eternal life believe. The word of the Lord spreads throughout the region. But the Jews stir up the devout women of prominence and the chief men of the city, raise persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and expel them from their borders. They shake off the dust of their feet against them and come to Iconium, and the disciples are filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
whySettingMatters: This begins what is usually called Paul's first missionary journey (about AD 46 to 48), and the book from here on follows Paul. The church at Antioch is multi-ethnic: Barnabas is from Cyprus, Simeon "Niger" (Latin for "black") may have been African, Lucius is from Cyrene in North Africa, and Manaen was raised with Herod Antipas. The Spirit sets Barnabas and Saul apart as the church fasts and worships. Cyprus was Barnabas' home island. The proconsul Sergius Paulus is probably the one named in inscriptions, and Luke correctly uses the title "proconsul" for the senatorial province. From verse 9 Saul is called Paul, using his Roman name; he now takes the lead, and the party is "Paul and his company." John Mark's departure at Perga becomes a cause of conflict in 15:36-40. Antioch of Pisidia was a Roman colony in central Asia Minor, with a synagogue; the order of service (reading the law and prophets, then a word of exhortation) matches Jewish practice. Paul's sermon is the longest example in Acts of a message to Jews and God-fearers, and follows the pattern of Stephen's but ends in Jesus and forgiveness. "As many as were appointed to eternal life believed" has been debated in the history of interpretation; the Greek word (tetagmenoi) can mean "appointed," "destined," or "disposed," and how much it says about God's choice is contested. Paul's turn to the Gentiles uses Isaiah 49:6, which Luke applied to Jesus in 2:32.

questions: The Spirit sets Barnabas and Saul apart as the church worships and fasts. What does that say about where mission starts?
Paul tells Israel's story and ends with Jesus. What does he want these hearers to see?
"We turn to the Gentiles." How much is this a decision, and how much a result of what happened in the synagogue?
"As many as were appointed to eternal life believed." How do you read that, and what does it assume about the one who reads it?
